question: A report from the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES)1 highlights the risks posed by isoflavones, which are naturally present in some plants. Isoflavones may have adverse effects on health, in particular on the reproductive system, if too many of them are consumed.

The report states that one of the main sources of isoflavones in our diets is soya, a legume that is often presented as a meat substitute on account of its high protein content. It is now recommended that soya-based foods should not be served in large-scale catering, in particular in school canteens.

ANSES invites those in industry and manufacturing to implement agronomic techniques and manufacturing processes that would make it possible to produce food while keeping isoflavone content under control. 1.
Given the health risks to consumers, does the Commission plan to review the labelling of soya-based products to highlight the dangers associated with eating them?

Given the need for further development of agronomic techniques and processes used to manufacture soya-based products in order to protect human health, does the Commission plan to reopen discussions with its main soya-supplying partners (Brazil, Argentina and the United States) in order to establish whether they will consider these recommendations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2025) The Commission is not planning a revision of the labelling rules for soya-based products at this stage. The Commission is aware of the opinion on health risks associated to the consumption of foods containing isoflavones issued by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety to which the Honourable Members refers.

In this respect, the Commission would like to point out that , while the opinion recommends that soya-based food should not be used in mass catering to avoid over-consumption and that food producers and manufacturers should review soya production and processing techniques in order to reduce isoflavone levels in food, it does not recommend establishing any specific labelling for soya-based foods.
Considering the above, there is currently no basis for seeking to address the issue with third countries at EU level.
